lesson_title: Bricks, a Balloon and Solar Panels: What Plant Cells Have That You Don't
hook_text: A plant cell is a brick house. Your cells are tents. Here are the three things the house has that the tent never will.
clip_script: Plant cell, animal cell. Same four basics: a membrane door, a cytoplasm floor, a nucleus office, mitochondria generators. Then three extras only the plant gets. One: brick walls. The cell wall, made of cellulose, the stuff of paper. It holds the plant up and makes the cells square, which is why onion cells look like bricks in rows. But the bricks are full of gaps, so the wall does not choose what comes in. The door still does. Two: a giant water balloon, the vacuole, full of cell sap. Full balloon, firm cell, upright plant. Empty balloon, soft cell, wilted lettuce. Put the lettuce in water and watch it crisp up again. Three: green solar panels, chloroplasts, packed with chlorophyll. Carbon dioxide plus water, add sunlight, out comes glucose and the oxygen you are breathing. But only in green parts. Onion bulbs grow in the dark, so no solar panels, and no green dots on your onion drawing. And the plant still keeps its generators: plants photosynthesise and respire. Your tent? Flexible, round, no bricks, no balloon, no panels. You eat instead.
visual_style: A brick house and a canvas tent side by side; bricks snap onto the house as the wall, a balloon inflates and deflates inside it while a lettuce droops and perks up, green panels appear on the roof and glow under a sun; an onion cell stays white.
pacing: Three equal beats for the three extras, a sharp stop on the onion trap, a one-line finish on the tent.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and fill the whole comparison table from memory.
